title: Does ordinary polynomial-hard LWE suffice for circuit obfuscation?
formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
definitions: Fix q(n) to be the least prime at least n^4 for every integer n≥2. Let χ_n be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to exp(−πe²/n²). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial m(n), the ensembles (A,A s+e mod q) and (A,u) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in Z_q^(m×n), s is uniform in Z_q^n, the m coordinates of e are independent χ_n samples, and u is independent uniform in Z_q^m. Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than n^(−c) eventually for every constant c>0. No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in λ+|C| that outputs a Boolean circuit O(1^λ,C) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible μ_p such that for every |C|≤p(λ), with probability at least 1−μ_p(λ) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences C_0,λ and C_1,λ with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated LWE-to-iO existence implication, allowing arbitrary non-black-box constructions and proofs, or refute that unrelativized implication. A result assuming subexponential hardness, a different LWE parameter regime, circular security, additional leakage resilience, pairings, or another independent assumption settles this card only if the extra requirement is derived from the specific LWE assumption here. A construction for a restricted circuit class or a barrier against one proof technique is partial progress.
context:
Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. This provides a plausible route to post-quantum obfuscation under the stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.
why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

importance.reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.

progress.text: Barak and coauthors establish impossibility for general virtual-black-box obfuscation while introducing weaker obfuscation notions, including the indistinguishability target.
Regev develops LWE, lattice-hardness connections and public-key encryption; these results supply the standard noisy-equation foundation, rather than general obfuscation.
Jain, Lin, and Sahai construct general iO from four well-founded assumptions with the quantitative security specified in their theorem. The JACM publication does not reduce the list to LWE.
Their follow-up removes LWE, obtaining iO from LPN over prime fields, DLIN, and local PRGs under subexponential security. It explicitly leaves minimal assumption sets open.

Brakerski and coauthors obtain iO from circular-security properties of LWE-based encryption, including randomness-leakage resilience. They also repair a limitation in a previous exponentially-efficient-obfuscation transformation.

references.locator: CRYPTO 2001; author page links subsequent full versions; virtual-black-box impossibility and weaker notions

references.locator: Author version 2 May 2009; STOC 2005 / JACM 2009; LWE definitions, lattice reductions and public-key cryptosystem. The exact polynomial parameters in this card are an explicit formulation choice.

references.authors: Aayush Jain; Huijia Lin; Amit Sahai
references.locator: Journal of the ACM 73(1), Article 1, 1–30, published 12 February 2026; Theorem 1.1 and §1.1 specify four assumptions and quantitative hardness

references.title: Indistinguishability Obfuscation from LPN over F_p, DLIN, and PRGs in NC^0
references.authors: Aayush Jain; Huijia Lin; Amit Sahai
references.locator: Introduction explicitly asks whether LWE alone suffices; main theorem removes LWE from the earlier sufficient set of assumptions

references.title: Factoring and Pairings Are Not Necessary for IO: Circular-Secure LWE Suffices
references.authors: Zvika Brakerski; Nico Döttling; Sanjam Garg; Giulio Malavolta
references.locator: ICALP 2022, 28:1–28:20; circular randomness-leakage resilience and corrected shallow-XiO transformation; full version ePrint 2020/1024

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.
